chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-01.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-01.body:
After the six other pirates have taken their shares, Alpha is left with
$$\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac45\cdot\tfrac78\cdot\tfrac{12}{13}\cdot\tfrac{20}{21}\,N=\tfrac8{39}N,$$
so $39\mid N$.

*Example with $3$ coins for Epsilon.* $N=39$ and the order Zeta, Gamma, Epsilon, Eta, Delta, Beta, Alpha gives stashes $39\to36\to24\to21\to20\to16\to8\to0$; Epsilon takes $24-21=3$.

*Lower bound.* After Epsilon's turn the stash is $\frac78$ of the stash before, hence a multiple of $7$; Epsilon's share is $\frac17$ of it. If Eta goes after Epsilon, the stash at Eta's turn is a multiple of $21$, so the stash after Epsilon is $\ge21$ and Epsilon received $\ge3$. If Eta goes before Epsilon, the stash after Epsilon is a multiple of $7$ and every later pirate (denominators $2,3,5,13$ coprime to $7$) keeps it a multiple of $7$, so Alpha's share $\frac8{39}N$ is a multiple of $7$; with $39\mid N$ this gives $\frac8{39}N\ge56$, the stash after Epsilon is $\ge56$ and Epsilon received at least $\frac{56}7=8\ge3$. So the minimum is $3$.

**Answer: 3**

chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-02.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-02.body:
Write $a_k=a_0+kx$ with $x\ne0$ ($a_0$ the 'zeroth' term), and note $a_1=a_0+x\ne0$. Geometric means $a_2^2=a_1a_n$ and $a_4^2=a_1a_p$:
$$(a_0+2x)^2=(a_0+x)(a_0+nx)\ \Rightarrow\ 4a_0+4x=(n+1)a_0+nx\ \Rightarrow\ n(a_0+x)=3a_0+4x,$$
$$(a_0+4x)^2=(a_0+x)(a_0+px)\ \Rightarrow\ 8a_0+16x=(p+1)a_0+px\ \Rightarrow\ p(a_0+x)=7a_0+16x.$$
Hence $n=3+\frac{x}{a_0+x}$ and $p=7+\frac{9x}{a_0+x}$, so $p=7+9(n-3)=9n-20$. Thus $c\cdot d=9\cdot(-20)=-180$.

**Answer: $-180$**

chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-03.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-03.body:
Over the five rotations, each digit is in its correct position exactly once, so the numbers of correct digits sum to $5$. The complement event is that every rotation has exactly one correct digit.

By rotation symmetry assume digit $1$ is correct in the initial position (24 equally likely arrangements) and the code is $1\text{-}2\text{-}3\text{-}4\text{-}5$. After one rotation step (shift right by one) the correct digit is $3$, $4$ or $5$ (not $1$ or $2$):
* correct digit $3$: input $1\,3\,x\,y\,z$; $y\ne4,5$ forces $y=2$, then $x=5$, $z=4$;
* correct digit $4$: input $1\,x\,4\,y\,z$; $x\ne2,3$ gives $x=5$, $y=3$, $z=2$;
* correct digit $5$: input $1\,x\,y\,5\,z$; $x=4$, $y=2$, $z=3$.
So $3$ of the $24$ arrangements fail, and the probability is $1-\frac3{24}=\frac78$ (each of those three indeed has exactly one correct digit per rotation).

**Answer: $\frac78$**

chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-04.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-04.body:
Add $a,b$ in binary with carries $c_i$ into position $i$ ($c_0=0$, digits $a_i,b_i$): $a_i+b_i+c_i=r_i+2c_{i+1}$ where $r_i$ are the digits of $a+b$. Then
$$f(a+b)-f(a)-f(b)=\sum_i\big(r_i-a_i-b_i\big)3^i=\sum_i(c_i-2c_{i+1})3^i=\sum_{j\ge1}c_j3^{j-1},$$
(because $\sum_i2c_{i+1}3^i=\tfrac23\sum_jc_j3^j$). So the values are the numbers whose base-$3$ digits are the carry bits $c_1,c_2,\dots\in\{0,1\}$. Every $0/1$ pattern of carries is realisable: if $c_j=0$ and we want $c_{j+1}=1$ take $a_j=b_j=1$, for $c_{j+1}=0$ take $a_j=b_j=0$; if $c_j=1$ and we want $c_{j+1}=1$ take $(a_j,b_j)=(1,0)$, for $c_{j+1}=0$ take $a_j=b_j=0$.

So the possible values are exactly the nonnegative integers with all base-$3$ digits in $\{0,1\}$. As $2026=2210001_3$ (7 digits), every positive number with at most $7$ digits $0/1$ is $\le1111111_3=1093<2026$, and any with $8$ digits is $\ge3^7=2187>2026$. The count is $2^7-1=127$.

**Answer: 127**

chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-05.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-05.body:
Let $a_{i,j}$ be the entries. *If row $i$ contains an adjacent equal pair* $a_{i,j}=a_{i,j+1}$, the $2\times2$ block at columns $j,j+1$ forces $a_{i+1,j}=a_{i+1,j+1}=1-a_{i,j}$. Given $a_{i+1,j}=1-a_{i,j}$, the block condition determines $a_{i+1,j+1}=2-a_{i,j}-a_{i,j+1}-a_{i+1,j}=1-a_{i,j+1}$, and likewise to the left; so row $i+1$ is the complement of row $i$ (which again has an adjacent equal pair). *If row $i$ is alternating*, each block forces $a_{i+1,j}+a_{i+1,j+1}=1$, so row $i+1$ is alternating too (either of the two alternating rows).

*Case 1: row 1 has two adjacent equal entries.* Then every row is the complement of the previous one, so the grid is determined by row 1, and every such grid works (each $2\times2$ block then has two $0$s and two $1$s). Row 1 can be any of $2^{10}$ rows except the two alternating rows: $2^{10}-2$ grids.

*Case 2: row 1 is $0101\cdots01$ or $1010\cdots10$.* Then every row is one of these two alternating rows, and any sequence of choices works: $2^{10}$ grids.

Total $2^{10}-2+2^{10}=2046$.

**Answer: 2046**

chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-06.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-06.body:
Let the parallelogram have centre $X$, distance $5$ from the pair of sides at distance $10$ apart and distance $7$ from the other pair; the angle between the sides is $\theta$ with $\frac{10\cdot14}{\sin\theta}=168$, so $\sin\theta=\frac56$.

The circle through the four feet has its centre on the perpendicular bisectors of the segments joining feet on opposite sides, which are the midlines of the parallelogram, so it is centred at $X$ with radius $\sqrt{50}$. It meets the sides at distance $5$ from $X$ in chords of length $2\sqrt{50-25}=10$ and the sides at distance $7$ in chords of length $2\sqrt{50-49}=2$.

Take orthonormal coordinates $(u,v)$ with origin $X$ and $AB$, $CD$ the lines $v=\mp5$. The circle $u^2+v^2=50$ meets them at $(\pm5,\mp5)$. The feet of $P$ on $AB$ and on $CD$ lie on the common line through $P$ perpendicular to them, so they have the same $u$-coordinate $\pm5$; hence $P$ lies on the line $u=5$ or $u=-5$ (two parallel lines at distance $10$).

Likewise the circle meets $BC$ and $DA$ in points at distance $1$ along the side from the foot of the perpendicular from $X$, and $P$ lies on one of two lines perpendicular to $BC$ at distance $1$ on either side of the perpendicular to $BC$ through $X$ (two parallel lines at distance $2$).

The four possible points $P$ are the four intersections of these two pairs of parallel lines. They form a parallelogram whose sides make the same angle $\theta$ as the sides of $ABCD$ (directions perpendicular to $AB$ and to $BC$), with 'heights' $10$ and $2$. Its area is $\frac{10\cdot2}{\sin\theta}=\frac{20}{5/6}=24$.

**Answer: 24**

chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-07.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-07.body:
Let $d_i=a_i-a_{i-1}\in\{6,7\}$. From $10$ steps summing to $67$: three $6$'s and seven $7$'s. Since $\gcd(a_i,a_{i+1})=\gcd(a_i,d_{i+1})$, the condition for $1\le i\le9$ is:
* step $i+1$ equals $7$: $7\nmid a_i$. With $s_i$ sixes among the first $i$ steps, $a_i=7i-s_i$, so this means $s_i\notin\{0,7\}$, i.e. at least one $6$ occurs before it;
* step $i+1$ equals $6$: $\gcd(a_i,6)=1$. Modulo $6$, $a_i\equiv i-s_i=u_i$, the number of $7$'s so far, so $u_i\in\{1,5,7\}$.
(For the first step ($i=0$) there is no condition.)

So a $6$ may be placed only (i) as the very first step, or (ii) in the gaps of the $7$'s after exactly $1$, $5$ or $7$ sevens (several $6$'s may sit in the same gap). And every $7$ at position $\ge2$ needs a $6$ earlier: so one of the first two steps must be a $6$, i.e. gap $0$ or gap $1$ gets a $6$.

Count: let $g_0\in\{0,1\}$ be the number of $6$'s at the start and $g_1,g_5,g_7\ge0$ in the other gaps with $g_0+g_1+g_5+g_7=3$. All solutions: $g_0=0$: $\binom52=10$; $g_0=1$: $\binom42=6$; total $16$. Remove those with $g_0=0$ and $g_1=0$ (no $6$ among the first two steps): $g_5+g_7=3$: $4$ solutions. Result $16-4=12$.

**Answer: 12**

chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-08.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-08.body:
From $\triangle BDC\sim\triangle ABC$: $\angle BCD=\angle ACB$; from $\triangle CBE\sim\triangle ABC$: $\angle CBE=\angle ABC$. So lines $CD$ and $BE$ pass through the reflection $A^*$ of $A$ in $BC$ (they make the same angles with $BC$ as $CA$, $BA$). Then $F$ is the intersection of the altitudes of $\triangle A^*BC$ from $B$ and $C$, i.e. its orthocenter, which is the reflection of the orthocenter of $ABC$ in $BC$; hence $F$ lies on line $AA^*$ and on the circumcircle of $ABC$.

The area ratios give $BC/AC=\sqrt2$ and $BC/AB=2$, so $AB:AC:BC=1:\sqrt2:2$. In the model triangle with sides $1,\sqrt2,2$: the foot $X$ of the altitude from $A$ has $XB=\frac{1+4-2}{4}=\frac34$, $XC=\frac54$, height $\frac{\sqrt7}4$, area $\frac{\sqrt7}4$. Scaling to area $1$ multiplies lengths by $\lambda=\frac{2}{7^{1/4}}$: $XA=\lambda\frac{\sqrt7}4$, $XB=\frac{3\lambda}4$, $XC=\frac{5\lambda}4$.

By the power of the point $X$ with respect to the circumcircle: $XF\cdot XA=XB\cdot XC$, so $XF=\frac{15\lambda}{4\sqrt7}$ and
$$AF=XA+XF=\lambda\Big(\frac{\sqrt7}4+\frac{15}{4\sqrt7}\Big)=\lambda\frac{11}{2\sqrt7}=\frac{11}{7^{3/4}}.$$
So $a+b=11+7=18$. (A coordinate computation confirms $AF\approx2.556=11/7^{3/4}$.)

**Answer: 18**

chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-10.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-10.body:
Height above the ground is an affine function. Let $v_1,v_2,v_3$ be the edge vectors from the lowest vertex (height $1$) and $d_i>0$ the corresponding height increments. The eight vertex heights are $1+\varepsilon_1d_1+\varepsilon_2d_2+\varepsilon_3d_3$, $\varepsilon_i\in\{0,1\}$, and they equal $1,\dots,8$. So the eight subset sums of $\{d_1,d_2,d_3\}$ are $0,\dots,7$: the smallest positive one is $1$, the next distinct is $2$, then $4$; thus $\{d_1,d_2,d_3\}=\{1,2,4\}$.

If $s$ is the side length and $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ the (unit) vertical direction in the cube's frame, then $d_i=s\,u_i$, and $u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2=1$. Hence $s^2=d_1^2+d_2^2+d_3^2=1+4+16=21$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{21}$**

chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-11.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-11.body:
Non-real roots come in conjugate pairs $c\pm di$, $e\pm fi$ ($d,f\ne0$). Then the polynomial is $(x^2-2cx+c^2+d^2)(x^2-2ex+e^2+f^2)$, so
$$69=(c^2+d^2)+(e^2+f^2)+4ce,\qquad100=(c^2+d^2)(e^2+f^2).$$
Let $\alpha=\sqrt{c^2+d^2}$, $\beta=\sqrt{e^2+f^2}$: $\alpha\beta=10$ and $|z_1|+\dots+|z_4|=2(\alpha+\beta)$. Since $|c|<\alpha$ and $|e|<\beta$, $4ce<4\alpha\beta=40$, so $69<\alpha^2+\beta^2+40$, i.e. $\alpha^2+\beta^2>29$ and $(\alpha+\beta)^2=\alpha^2+\beta^2+20>49$, $\alpha+\beta>7$. The sum exceeds $14$.

It can be made arbitrarily close to $14$: take $\alpha\to2$, $\beta\to5$ (so $\alpha\beta=10$, $\alpha^2+\beta^2=29$), $c\approx\alpha$, $e\approx\beta$, with $d,f\to0$ so that $4ce\to40$ and the equation $69=\dots$ holds. Hence $m=14$.

**Answer: 14**

chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-12.title: Markov chain
Solve
chmmc-cmm-2026-individual-12.body:
For $n\ge2$: $a_n=1+\frac18a_{n-1}+\frac14a_n+\frac18a_{n+1}$, i.e. $b_n=a_n-2$ satisfies $b_n=\frac16(b_{n-1}+b_{n+1})$ for $n\ge2$. The solutions are $b_n=c_1(3+2\sqrt2)^n+c_2(3-2\sqrt2)^n$ for $n\ge1$, and boundedness forces $c_1=0$; with $\rho=3-2\sqrt2$: $a_2=2+\rho(a_1-2)$. The other equations are $a_0=1+\frac14a_0+\frac34a_1\Rightarrow a_0=a_1+\frac43$ and $a_1=1+\frac12a_1+\frac18a_0+\frac18a_2\Rightarrow a_2=3a_1-\frac{28}3$. Substituting: $a_1(3-\rho)=\frac{34}3-2\rho$, $a_1=\frac{16/3+4\sqrt2}{2\sqrt2}=2+\frac{4\sqrt2}3$. Hence $a_0=\frac{10+4\sqrt2}3\approx5.219$.

**Answer: $\frac{10+4\sqrt2}{3}$**
